planting.note: Plant container-grown saplings in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil at a woodland edge or beneath high open canopy; seed needs several months of cold stratification and is slow and unreliable to germinate, so nursery stock is the practical starting point.

directions: Site this slender understory tree where it gets filtered morning sun or dappled light all day, in loamy soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged. Once established, harvest the tightly furled terminal buds just as they begin to open each spring, snapping them off the way you would pick asparagus tips. The buds carry a clean, faintly bitter, almost nutty flavor prized across Japan for tempura and quick blanching, and many foragers rank it above other spring shoots for its delicacy. Because it thrives in the dappled light beneath larger trees, it fills a niche few other food crops can occupy in a wooded garden.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant divisions or seedlings in spring into ordinary, moisture-retentive garden soil at a woodland edge or under high shade; established clumps spread by rhizome and are easiest to propagate by dividing an existing patch rather than starting from seed.

directions: Grow yomogi in loose, humus-rich soil in the light shade beneath deciduous trees, where its silvery-backed leaves stay tender and less coarse than plants grown in full sun. Cut the youngest leaf tips repeatedly through spring and early summer before flowering begins, since older leaves turn tough and bitter. The finely chopped, blanched leaves give kusa mochi and other Japanese rice sweets their deep green color and a distinctive herbal, slightly resinous flavor, and the dried leaf is also steeped as tea. It spreads by rhizome, so give it a bounded bed or a large container if you want to keep its cheerful colonizing habit in check.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant divisions into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil at a woodland margin in early spring; established clumps can also be divided in fall to start new plantings.

directions: Plant chwinamul in cool, humus-rich soil under the broken light of deciduous trees, where the broad basal leaves stay tender longer than they do in open sun. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips repeatedly through spring; a quick blanch mellows their mild, herbal, faintly sesame-like flavor before they are tossed with sesame oil, garlic, and soy for the classic Korean namul side dish. It is one of the most widely grown wild greens in Korean home gardens precisely because it tolerates the shady, moist corners where lettuce and other sun-loving greens struggle. Left unharvested in late summer it produces small white daisy-like flowers that draw pollinators to the shade garden.
sources: Rural Development Administration of Korea (National Institute of Horticultural and Herbal Science)

planting.note: Plant divisions or stem cuttings in spring into ordinary, well-drained soil at the edge of a shaded bed; this tough succulent roots readily from broken stem pieces and tolerates lean soil poorly suited to leafier vegetables.

directions: Orpine grows happily in light shade beneath shrubs or trees, tolerating drier, leaner soil than most edible greens, and its thick gray-green leaves hold moisture the way its Sedum relatives do. Pinch young leaves and stem tips through the growing season and add them raw to salads for a crisp, faintly lemony, cucumber-like bite, or steam them briefly as a minor cooked green in the old Northern and Eastern European tradition of eating this plant. Because it needs so little water and shrugs off shade that defeats lettuce and spinach, it earns a spot in the low-input corners of a woodland food garden. Deadhead the pink late-summer flower clusters if you prefer to keep the plant compact and leafy.

planting.note: Plant root divisions or container stock in spring into deep, humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil under high open shade; seed germinates slowly after cold stratification, so divisions from an established crown are the faster route to a harvestable clump.

directions: This robust herbaceous perennial dies back to a woody crown each winter and pushes up thick new shoots in spring that are harvested young, before the huge compound leaves fully expand, in the same manner as Japanese angelica tree shoots. Peel and blanch the shoots to soften a mild, resinous bitterness, then stir-fry or season with sesame oil for a classic Korean spring vegetable known as dokwallamul. The root has a long history in Korean herbal medicine as well, though it is the tender shoots that make it worth growing in a shaded vegetable bed. Give it deep, rich soil and generous moisture and it will return reliably for many years from the same crown.
sources: Rural Development Administration of Korea (National Institute of Horticultural and Herbal Science)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in deep, moist, humus-rich soil beneath high canopy or on a woodland edge; fresh seed needs several months of cold stratification and germinates unevenly, so nursery-grown plants are the more reliable start.

directions: Give this large, coarse-leaved shrub a sheltered spot with dappled or half-day shade and consistently moist, rich soil, mimicking the Himalayan and Chinese forest margins it comes from. By autumn, established plants hang thick with startling metallic-blue, finger-like seed pods several inches long; split one open to reach the sweet, translucent, gelatinous pulp inside, which tastes something like watermelon or lychee, though the numerous black seeds must be spit out. It needs a male and female plant, or a self-fertile seedling, to set the curious pods reliably. Few other fruiting shrubs offer both genuine shade tolerance and such a conversation-starting harvest.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring against a shaded wall, fence, or understory trellis in rich, well-drained soil; semi-hardwood cuttings taken in summer root more reliably than seed for this evergreen climber.

directions: This evergreen woody vine is unusual among fruiting plants for genuinely preferring shade to partial shade, making it one of the few climbers suited to a north-facing wall or the dim understory of a garden pergola. Train the twining stems onto a trellis or fence and be patient, since named or grafted plants fruit far sooner than seedlings, which can take years to bear. In autumn the vine produces oblong purple fruit similar to its relative akebia, splitting to reveal a sweet, milky-white pulp studded with small black seeds that is eaten fresh by hand in Japan. Plant two vines for best pollination and fruit set, since a single plant fruits sparsely on its own.

planting.note: Plant container stock or rhizome divisions in spring into acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil under the broken canopy of conifers or tall deciduous trees; wild seed germinates poorly, so divisions or nursery plants establish far more reliably.

directions: Mountain huckleberry naturally colonizes the filtered light beneath conifer forests in the Pacific Northwest and Rockies, so give it acidic soil, steady moisture, and the dappled shade of nearby trees rather than open, exposed sun. Established plants spread slowly by underground rhizomes and reward patience with intensely flavored, dark purple berries in late summer that are considered by many foragers to be the finest of all the huckleberries for pies, jam, and eating fresh. It is notoriously slow to establish from nursery stock, so plant it where it can be left undisturbed for years. This is a true forest-floor crop, offering a genuinely shade-adapted alternative to sun-loving blueberries.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring into cool, acidic, consistently moist, humus-rich soil beneath spruce, hemlock, or other conifer canopy; this species tolerates deeper shade than most Vaccinium and is best started from nursery-propagated plants rather than seed.

directions: Native across the cool coniferous forests of Alaska, the Pacific Northwest, and northern Japan, this blueberry relative is remarkably tolerant of dense shade and thrives in the same acidic, mossy understory conditions that defeat most fruiting shrubs. Its pale pink spring flowers give way to soft blue berries by midsummer, among the earliest wild blueberries to ripen, with a mild sweet flavor traditionally gathered fresh or dried by Indigenous peoples of the Pacific coast and interior. Keep the soil consistently moist and acidic and avoid any lime or wood ash near the roots. For a genuinely shade-loving berry crop under established evergreens, this species outperforms almost any cultivated blueberry.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System
University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or container canes in spring into rich, well-drained soil at a partially shaded forest edge or under high canopy; this bramble suckers readily, and new canes lifted with roots attached transplant more reliably than seed.

directions: This slender, nearly thornless bramble stays compact and shrubby rather than sprawling, and it holds its foliage through mild winters where hardy, making it useful as a shade-tolerant edge planting under fruit trees or along a woodland path. It flowers and fruits nearly continuously in warm climates, producing small, soft, sweet-tart red raspberries that are eaten fresh, though they are more delicate and less productive per cane than temperate raspberries. Give it half-day shade and evenly moist soil, and thin out older canes each year to keep new fruiting wood coming. It offers gardeners in humid subtropical and tropical shade gardens a genuine raspberry-family fruit where classic raspberries fail from heat stress.
sources: University of Hawaii at Manoa Cooperative Extension
